What to Watch in H2 2026: Catalysts, Risks and Election Calendar

The second half of 2026 pivots around four sequential catalysts. In July, the USMCA mid-term review defines the direction for Mexican equities and for the broader nearshoring narrative. In August, Colombia holds its presidential election, effectively closing the Petro era and opening a potential COLCAP re-rating toward the 2,600-plus zone if a market-oriented successor prevails. In October, Brazil’s presidential election will shape the post-Lula equity narrative and test investor confidence in policy continuity. Through all of it, every Copom, BanRep and Banxico meeting will be judged against a single question: how quickly can Latin America cut rates without reigniting inflation?

The bull-case framework is anchored by Morgan Stanley. The bank sees the MSCI Latin America Index rising more than 90% by 2030, and capital markets tripling from $2.4 trillion in 2024 to $6.3 trillion by 2035, driven by declining rates, pro-investment election outcomes and supply-chain realignment, per its March 2026 outlook note. Within that frame, Morgan Stanley’s 13,700 IPSA target and bullish Brazilian real forecast (30% appreciation potential, with equity AUM potentially jumping from $100 billion to $600 billion by 2035) are the most concrete published objectives.

The bear-case voices are headed by the World Bank, which trimmed 2026 regional growth to 2.1% from 2.4% in 2025, citing the Iran shock, elevated borrowing costs and weak external demand. Brazil GDP is pegged at 1.6%, Mexico at 1.3%. For investors positioning for the back half of the year, the operative questions are whether Hormuz fully reopens (the normalization trade favors LatAm ex-energy), whether Colombia’s election produces a market-oriented president, whether the USMCA review delivers ratification, and whether Argentine earnings growth finally catches up with reform-driven valuation expansion. Sector winners most frequently cited include energy (Petrobras, Ecopetrol, YPF), Brazilian banks (Itaú, Bradesco, Santander Brasil), Chilean copper plays, MercadoLibre’s fintech and e-commerce footprint, and Mexican nearshoring industrials.

The risk register deserves equal airtime. A re-escalation of the Iran conflict and renewed Hormuz closure would slam Chile (oil importer), put pressure on Mexican and Brazilian central banks through fertilizer- and LNG-linked inflation, and likely trigger a global equity sell-off that would pull LatAm down with it — even though net oil exporters would receive fiscal relief. A re-acceleration of Brazilian IPCA would force the Copom to pause or even reverse cuts, undermining the disinflation-plus-easing story that has drawn foreign capital. A China growth shock would compress both iron ore (hitting Vale) and copper (hitting Chile). And political risk sits over all five markets: Brazil’s October election will test policy continuity; Colombia’s August vote is binary for COLCAP; Mexico’s USMCA review has three distinct outcomes; Argentina’s reform program must deliver tangible earnings translation; and Chile, while politically stable today, faces congressional gridlock that could slow corporate tax cuts.

For investors building new LatAm exposure now, the diversification argument is compelling. The five benchmarks are driven by genuinely different catalysts — Brazilian carry and oil, Argentine reform, Colombian politics, Chilean copper, Mexican trade — which means correlations within the region can drop meaningfully in response to country-specific news. A blended position (EWZ + ARGT + ECH + EWW, with a tactical COLO/GXG sleeve) offers exposure to all five stories at different weights. The ILF ETF accomplishes much the same at a single-ticker level, albeit with a heavy Brazil tilt. The central risk to avoid is confusing local-currency gains (Merval +22.9% ARS) with dollar-terms wealth creation: peso dynamics can erase headline returns for international investors, and hedged share classes or direct ETF expression tend to be cleaner vehicles than ADRs of individual Argentine names.

The Commodity Supercycle Running Underneath Every LatAm Index

Step back from individual tickers and a single thread runs through every LatAm index: a genuine commodity supercycle. Copper breached $6/lb for the first time ever in January 2026, averaging $5.85 in the first six days of the year versus $3.97 in the same period of 2025. The global copper market is projected to run a 150,000-tonne deficit in 2026, and the energy-transition bid — EV batteries, solar, wind turbines, grid buildout — is expected to drive roughly a 70% increase in demand by 2050. That is the structural rationale behind Chile’s $104.5 billion investment pipeline, of which 89.8% is earmarked specifically for copper projects.

Oil sits alongside copper. Even before the Iran shock, Latin America was set to deliver 700,000-800,000 barrels per day of new non-OPEC supply in 2026, anchored by Brazil’s pre-salt production ramp toward a ~5 million bpd goal by 2030, Guyana’s continued streaming growth, and Argentina’s Vaca Muerta shale complex. Hormuz uncertainty has added a geopolitical-premium bid to Hormuz-free barrels, and LPG exports from Argentina doubled to roughly 50 million tonnes into India after the March shock. Ecopetrol’s 121% reserve-replacement ratio in 2025 was better than feared given Petro’s exploration moratorium.

Iron ore and agricultural commodities round out the picture. Vale’s iron ore exposure has been volatile on China signals, but a resumption of Chinese stimulus could reprice the stock sharply. Fertilizer dislocations from Hormuz continue to work through Brazilian agri supply chains, with knock-on inflation implications. The Global Economics characterization of LatAm 2026 as a genuine commodity supercycle year is consistent with the price action across copper, oil, and softer commodities, and it is a major reason the region’s equity markets have decoupled from the U.S. large-cap complex for the first sustained stretch in many years.

World.title: Iran War and Hormuz Crisis 2026: Oil, Latin America and the Global Fallout
World.content:
The Rio Times In-Depth Series

The 2026 Iran War has delivered the largest oil-supply shock in modern history, closing the Strait of Hormuz, sending Brent crude to a $128-a-barrel peak and cutting global petroleum flows by more than 10 million barrels per day. For Latin America, the fallout is a split-screen story: an oil and commodity windfall for Brazil, Colombia and Argentina on one side, and a fertilizer, diesel and food-price crunch that is reshaping the region’s 2026 economic outlook on the other.

Key Points U.S.-Israel Operation Epic Fury began February 28, 2026, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the opening strike and running 38 days before an April 7–8 ceasefire mediated by Pakistan.

Brent crude surged roughly 55% in March 2026 — a record monthly gain — peaking near $128 on April 2 before settling around $93 after the ceasefire.

Strait of Hormuz throughput collapsed from ~20 million bpd to just 3.8 million bpd by April 13, with only about 7 tankers transiting per day versus a pre-war average of 140.

The IEA calls March’s 10.1 million bpd supply loss the largest disruption in the history of the global oil market; 400 million barrels have been released from emergency reserves.

Brazil’s Ibovespa ended Q1 2026 up 16.35% with R$48 billion in foreign inflows, while the real strengthened toward a two-year high near 5.15 per dollar.

Brazilian urea prices jumped 35% in early March and 36% of urea imports came from the war zone, threatening the 2026/2027 crop season.

Brazil’s exports to the Middle East fell 26% in March, from $1.2 billion to $882 million, with corn and grain shipments hit hardest.

A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports took effect April 13 after the Islamabad Talks collapsed; the two-week ceasefire expires April 21, 2026.

When the first American and Israeli cruise missiles struck Tehran at 9:45 a.m. Iran time on February 28, 2026, they set in motion the most consequential energy-market event since the 1973 oil embargo. Within 12 hours, roughly 900 strikes had decimated Iran’s air defenses, missile inventories and command structure — and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was dead in his own office, according to the Wikipedia chronology of the 2026 Iran war. Within five days, the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed. Within a month, Brent crude had risen 55%, American gasoline had crossed $4 a gallon for the first time in more than two years, and a Brazilian farmer in Mato Grosso was paying 35% more for the urea that fertilizes his next corn crop.

This pillar unpacks how the Iran War and the Hormuz crisis reshaped 2026 — from the tactical surprise of Operation Epic Fury to the ceasefire negotiated in Islamabad, from the intraday $128 spike in Brent to the tortilla-price ripple in Mexico City, and from Petrobras’s windfall to the R$0.32-per-liter diesel subsidy the Lula government rolled out to keep Brazilian inflation from spiraling. The lens is Latin American, but the lesson is global: a 38-day war has rewritten the terms of trade for every country in the Western Hemisphere.

How the War Began: From Failed Talks to Operation Epic Fury

The path to February 28 ran through a year of failed diplomacy. President Donald Trump had sent a letter to Supreme Leader Khamenei in April 2025 with a 60-day deadline for a nuclear agreement. That deadline passed. Talks resumed in Oman, Rome and Geneva through the autumn of 2025 and collapsed over the same sticking point every time: Washington demanded full dismantlement of Iran’s enrichment program; Tehran insisted enrichment was non-negotiable, as documented in the diplomatic record of the 2025–2026 negotiations.

The political situation inside Iran deteriorated catastrophically in early 2026. On December 28, 2025, the largest protests since the 1979 revolution erupted over economic despair and regime mismanagement. On January 8, 2026, Iranian security forces launched a brutal crackdown; the Iranian Ministry of Health itself would later acknowledge at least 30,000 civilian deaths. Trump responded on January 12 with a 25% tariff on all goods from countries doing business with Iran and began the largest U.S. military buildup in the Middle East since the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

The final round of indirect talks took place in Muscat on February 6, 2026 — no agreement. On February 17, Khamenei publicly rejected U.S. terms. On February 25, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi declared in Geneva that a “historic” agreement was “within reach.” Washington walked out. Two days later, aboard Air Force One en route to Corpus Christi, Texas, Trump ordered the operation.

Operation Epic Fury — the Israeli component was called Operation Roaring Lion — was designed for tactical surprise precisely because it launched during active negotiations. In the first 12 hours, U.S. and Israeli forces conducted approximately 900 strikes. The Israeli Air Force flew roughly 200 jets simultaneously against some 500 Iranian targets — the largest single sortie in IAF history. Over 1,200 bombs were dropped in the first 24 hours. Cyberattacks caused a near-total internet blackout across Iran for more than 60 hours. One strike on a naval base near Minab killed roughly 160 civilians when it hit an adjacent girls’ school.

By 2:30 a.m. Eastern time on February 28, Trump had posted a Truth Social statement that Middle East analysts read as a thinly-veiled call for regime change. Iran responded that afternoon with Operation True Promise IV, launching hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles at Israel, U.S. bases in Qatar, Bahrain and Iraq, and Gulf Arab capitals including Manama, Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. The first commercial tanker strikes in the Strait of Hormuz began the same day. For a detailed operational account, our report on Trump’s Hormuz blockade order after the Islamabad talks collapse captures the April aftershocks.

The speed of the opening strike was unprecedented. U.S. B-2 bombers staging from Diego Garcia and Whiteman Air Force Base coordinated with Israeli F-35s, F-15Is and F-16s, with carrier-based F/A-18s from the USS Gerald R. Ford strike group providing suppression of enemy air defenses. Tomahawk cruise missiles fired from U.S. destroyers in the Arabian Sea and Eastern Mediterranean hit fixed command centers in the opening salvo. On March 2, Iran-backed Hezbollah launched attacks into northern Israel, attempting to open a second front; Israel responded with what analysts have called the most intensive suppression of Hezbollah capabilities since 2006. A U.S. KC-135 tanker went down over western Iraq on March 12, killing six airmen — the single largest U.S. loss of the war. On March 4, a U.S. submarine sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena off Sri Lanka, killing more than 104 crew members. Two days later, on March 6, the Israeli Air Force shot down an Iranian Yak-130 fighter jet over Tehran — the first air-to-air combat kill for the F-35 and the first Israeli air-to-air kill since 1985.

Timeline: 38 Days That Moved Every Market on Earth

Date Event Market Impact Feb 28 Operation Epic Fury begins; Khamenei killed Brent opens $72 → $80–82 within days Mar 4 IRGC announces closure of Strait of Hormuz; QatarEnergy declares force majeure on LNG Brent $83; LNG spot +30% Mar 8 Mojtaba Khamenei named Supreme Leader Iran leadership continuity locked in Mar 12 Brazil eliminates federal diesel taxes, imposes 12% crude export levy Petrobras volatility; real rallies Mar 14 U.S. strikes Kharg Island (90% of Iranian oil exports) Brent $95+ Mar 18 Iran strikes Qatar’s Ras Laffan LNG complex Asian LNG +140%; TTF near €60/MWh Mar 22 Trump issues 48-hour Hormuz ultimatum Brent crosses $110 on Mar 27 Mar 28 Houthis launch first direct missiles at Israel Shipping risk premium spikes Mar 31 Brent ends record 55% monthly surge; WTI over $100 U.S. gasoline $4/gal; California above $5 Apr 2 Brent intraday peak ~$128 Ibovespa 187,952; USD/BRL 5.15 Apr 7–8 Two-week ceasefire announced (Pakistan-mediated) Brent −15% to ~$93.82 Apr 10–12 Islamabad Talks end without agreement Oil range-bound $90–95 Apr 13 U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports takes effect Hormuz flows at 3.8 mbpd vs 20 pre-war Apr 16 Israel–Lebanon 10-day truce announced Second Islamabad round under discussion

By the time the ceasefire took effect at dawn on April 8 in the Gulf, the White House was declaring victory in a statement titled “Peace Through Strength: Operation Epic Fury Crushes Iranian Threat.” The tally from 38 days of major combat: more than 10,200 U.S. air sorties, over 13,000 targets struck, 150-plus Iranian naval vessels destroyed, 13 American service members killed. A coalition led by Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Army Chief General Asim Munir, with Turkey and Egypt assisting, brokered the pause.

The Strait of Hormuz: How Iran’s Closure Choked Global Shipping

Roughly 20 million barrels per day of crude oil and refined products move through the Strait of Hormuz in normal times — about 20% of global petroleum liquids. Another 20% of global liquefied natural gas passes the same narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman. Before the war, between 129 and 140 ships transited each day.

Iran’s closure strategy, announced by the IRGC on March 4, was notable for what it did not include: there was no immediate mining of the strait. Instead, Iran conducted drone strikes near commercial tankers and issued public warnings that any ships attempting to navigate “would be set ablaze.” Within days, war-risk insurers refused coverage, and the strait effectively closed on its own. As Time Magazine documented in its April 7 report, Iran carved out a two-corridor system: an IRGC-controlled northern corridor and a negotiated southern corridor along the Omani coast, with tolls of up to $2 million per vessel proposed.

By April 10, only about 7 tankers were transiting the strait daily — a 95% collapse from pre-war levels. The International Energy Agency reported on April 13 that flows through Hormuz had fallen to just 3.8 million barrels per day. Iran selectively permitted passage to vessels from China, Turkey, Pakistan and India in exchange for political and commercial concessions — a dynamic that gave Beijing, in particular, remarkable leverage over the post-war oil map.

The strategic logic behind Iran’s approach was cold-blooded. Foreign policy analyst Richard Haass, writing on Substack on March 18, articulated what became the central Iranian doctrine: the Strait of Hormuz must be “open for all or closed to all.” By selectively permitting certain flags and blocking others, Iran forced every importing nation to negotiate bilaterally with Tehran — effectively converting the strait from a neutral international waterway into a toll road under Iranian sovereignty. The proposed $2 million per-vessel fee, split with Oman, was designed to fund Iranian reconstruction while generating a de facto Iranian veto over global energy flows. U.S. CENTCOM began mine-clearance operations in mid-April after Iranian naval sources acknowledged that some mines had been “lost” during the opening strikes — a claim the Pentagon viewed with significant skepticism.

Gulf producers—Saudi Arabia, Iraq, UAE and Kuwait—collectively cut output by 6.7 million bpd by March 10 and by more than 10 million bpd by March 12, according to aggregated tanker-tracking data. Even producers not directly struck, such as Saudi Aramco’s Eastern Province operations, saw shipment delays as war-risk insurance became prohibitively expensive. Hapag-Lloyd CEO Rolf Habben Jansen captured the carrier industry view: the problem will not be solved “until all the ships have left the Strait.” Approximately 200 ships were reported wandering in the Persian Gulf region at the height of the disruption, unable to load cargo or to exit through contested waters.

The container-shipping market seized up in parallel. More than 400,000 TEU of global container capacity was trapped inside the Persian Gulf — roughly 1.4% of the world fleet. War-risk surcharges hit $4,000 per container. Ships bound for U.S. East Coast ports rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope, adding 10–14 days of transit. Hundreds of thousands of containers piled up at Indian, Omani and Pakistani ports waiting for safe passage. Even under the most optimistic scenario, Kpler shipping analytics estimates oil flows will not normalize until July 2026, with the container backlog stretching into Q3 or Q4.

The Oil Price Shock: Brent’s Record 55% March Surge

Brent crude entered February 2026 at roughly $72.48. The Energy Information Administration’s pre-war forecast had called for a 2026 average of $78.84. By the end of March, Brent had surged 55% — a record monthly gain — and the monthly average for March came in at $103 per barrel, according to the Wikipedia dossier on the 2026 Iran war fuel crisis.

The intraday peak came on April 2, when Brent briefly touched $127.90 and WTI crossed $115. The April 8 ceasefire announcement triggered a roughly 15% one-day drop, with Brent settling near $93.82. By mid-April, both benchmarks were trading in the $90–95 range — still about 30–35% above pre-war levels, but well below the panic peaks. The EIA revised its 2026 Brent forecast to $96 per barrel on April 8, with WTI at $87.41. As our coverage of how oil surged past $85 as the Hormuz crisis choked global supply documented, the market’s psychology flipped overnight on every ceasefire rumor.

Date Brent WTI Driver Feb 27 $72.48 $68.00 Pre-war close Mar 5 $83.00 $79.00 Hormuz closure confirmed Mar 27 $112.57 $108.00 Houthis enter conflict Apr 2 (peak) ~$128 $115.48 Intraday spike Apr 8 $93.82 $91.20 Ceasefire announcement Apr 16 ~$92 $90.59–93.47 Blockade stalemate

The physical market tells a harsher story than the futures market. The IEA declared March’s 10.1 million bpd supply loss — 9% of global supply — the largest disruption in the recorded history of the global oil market. Member states released a record 400 million barrels from emergency reserves in a coordinated drawdown. Even so, the agency’s executive director warned in April that futures prices “still do not reflect the severity of the crisis.” Global oil demand, the IEA now forecasts, will contract by 80,000 bpd in 2026 — the first annual decline since the 2020 Covid shock.

Natural gas markets moved even more violently. When Iran struck Qatar’s Ras Laffan Industrial City LNG complex on March 18, it knocked out 17% of Qatari production capacity — damage requiring 3–5 years to repair. Asian LNG spot prices surged more than 140%, reaching $25.40 per MMBtu, a three-year high. Europe’s Dutch TTF benchmark nearly doubled from its pre-war baseline of roughly €30/MWh to above €60/MWh by mid-March. QatarEnergy, which supplies roughly 20% of global LNG, declared force majeure on all contracts.

Brazil: Oil Windfall Meets Fertilizer Crisis

No country in Latin America has been more sharply split by the Iran War than Brazil. As the world’s sixth-largest oil exporter — producing 3.7 million bpd — Brazil’s treasury is a direct beneficiary of higher Brent. The Ministry of Finance estimates that sustained $100 Brent translates into additional government revenue worth nearly 1% of GDP compared with the 2026 budget baseline. Petrobras shares spiked on the war’s opening and remained volatile around every ceasefire rumor — dropping 2.67% on April 2, for instance, as Brent slid toward $101.

Brazil’s ethanol infrastructure provides an extraordinary consumer shock absorber. With a 30% mandatory blend in gasoline and universal flex-fuel vehicles, Brazilian pump prices rose only about 5% in March against a 30% jump in the United States, as documented in AP News’s analysis of Brazil’s unique insulation. The record sugarcane harvest beginning in April is projected to yield 30 billion liters of ethanol. Our feature on Brazil’s ethanol as an energy shield in the Iran oil crisis examines how decades of biofuel investment are now paying strategic dividends.

But Brazil imports roughly 25% of the diesel it consumes, and diesel prices surged more than 20% in March. Because Brazilian agricultural logistics depend overwhelmingly on trucking, diesel inflation feeds directly into food prices. On March 12, the Lula government responded with a package: eliminating federal diesel taxes (PIS/Cofins), imposing a 12% export levy on crude, a 50% tax on diesel exports and a direct R$0.32-per-liter diesel subsidy effective through December 2026. QAV (jet fuel) rose 55% effective April 1, adding pressure on domestic aviation.

The fertilizer side of the equation is where Brazil’s vulnerability is most acute. Brazil is the world’s largest fertilizer importer and sources all three primary nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium — from overseas. According to Agrinvest data, 41% of Brazil’s urea imports transited the Strait of Hormuz before the war; 36% originated in the war zone itself (Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Oman, UAE). Brazilian urea prices jumped 35% in the first weeks of March. For operational cost structures, fertilizers represent 34% of summer corn costs, 30% of wheat, and 27% of soybeans and second-crop corn. As our report on the Colombia fertilizer crisis and Hormuz-driven food inflation details, the same dynamics cascade across the Andean economies.

Brazil’s potential phosphate deficit is estimated at 1–3 million tons — roughly 20% of total demand — and 78% of Brazilian phosphate consumption is imported. Industry analysts warn that if fertilizer access remains restricted through September, the 2026/2027 crop season faces serious shortage risk, with direct consequences for global soybean and corn supply. Brazil accounts for roughly 60% of global soybean exports and is the world’s largest beef exporter.

Brazilian Markets: Ibovespa’s Record Q1, a Real Near Two-Year Highs

Paradoxically, Brazilian financial markets have had one of their best quarters in years. The Ibovespa ended Q1 2026 up 16.35%, with R$48 billion in foreign inflows — the strongest first quarter in recent memory. A February 25 peak of 192,624 was revisited and exceeded in mid-April, with the index trading in the 197,000–199,000 range. The war produced an intra-market rotation: banks and industrials rallied on de-escalation hopes, while Petrobras sold off when oil fell. Our coverage of the Ibovespa approaching 198K on Iran-deal hopes and Ibovespa ceasefire-day banks rallying as Petrobras fell captures the daily swings.

The Brazilian real strengthened to roughly 5.15 per U.S. dollar by early April — a near two-year high — outperforming the entire emerging-markets currency complex on the back of commodity export windfalls. HSBC analysts wrote that “Latin American currencies are being favored in the emerging market context” relative to their Asian and European peers. The real has faced pressure in risk-off sessions, but its underlying story is one of structural strength from high terms of trade.

Inflation and monetary policy are the counterweights. Annual Brazilian inflation edged to 4.14% in March 2026, above the 3.9% mid-month IPCA-15 estimate and above the official target, driven primarily by fuel costs. The Central Bank slowed its rate-cut pace, cutting just 25 basis points in March to bring the Selic to 14.75%, with the Focus survey consensus now seeing a year-end Selic at 12.25%. Brazil’s Treasury chief warned Reuters that the Iran conflict could shorten the rate-cut cycle, a scenario that would complicate Lula’s fiscal calculations heading into his final legislative push.

Brazil’s Trade with the Middle East: A 26% Collapse

Brazilian exports to the Middle East fell 26% in March 2026, from $1.2 billion in March 2025 to $882 million, according to Ministry of Development, Industry and Trade data published by DatamarNews. Corn was the headline casualty — approximately 25% of Brazil’s corn exports go to Middle Eastern buyers, a pipeline now near-frozen. Brazil has struck an emergency deal with Turkey for transit and temporary storage of agribusiness goods bound for Middle East and Central Asian markets, but the logistics are expensive and slow. China-bound oil flows have partly compensated, as our reporting on Brazil’s record Q1 2026 oil exports to China driven by the Hormuz disruption shows.

The Turkey deal is worth examining in detail. Brazilian meat processors (JBS, BRF, Marfrig) and grain exporters (Amaggi, SLC Agrícola, Bunge) have shifted Middle East-bound cargo to Turkish ports for transit storage and final-leg delivery. The arrangement costs Brazilian exporters an estimated 8–12% in additional logistics and handling, but preserves market access. For sugar, coffee and pulp, China and India have absorbed the reshuffled volumes. Saudi Arabia’s food-security reserves, which Brazil helped build out during 2020–2023, are being drawn down aggressively; Riyadh’s sovereign purchasing arm has signaled willingness to pay a substantial premium to keep strategic inventories stocked. The net effect on Brazilian agribusiness has been a revenue hit but a margin-preservation story, thanks to higher global prices offsetting lower Middle East volumes.

Argentina: Vaca Muerta Tailwinds Meet Fertilizer Headwinds

For Argentina, the Iran War is an ambivalent shock. The Vaca Muerta unconventional oil field in Patagonia becomes dramatically more economic at $90-plus Brent, and President Javier Milei’s government has been accelerating licensing and export infrastructure to capitalize. At the same time, agriculture accounts for roughly 60% of Argentine exports — and agriculture is squeezed on both ends. Iran alone produces about 15% of world urea, and global fertilizer prices are rising sharply. Argentine farmers face higher input costs even as they benefit from elevated global grain prices.

The macro story is more nuanced. Global instability typically drives capital flight from emerging markets, and Argentina’s FX reserves remain thin. A Citi research note flagged peso-depreciation risk from war-driven risk-off flows. Yet the opposite has largely held: Argentine carry-trade positions have performed well, with high local rates compensating for macro uncertainty. Our deep dive into the Argentine peso carry trade during the Iran War and its implications for emerging markets unpacks the mechanics. Record 2026 crop yields are expected, but margin pressure from surging fuel and fertilizer costs could compress farm income substantially.

Colombia, Chile, Mexico and Venezuela: The Rest of Latin America’s Split

Colombia sits in the middle. Crude oil accounts for about 25% of Colombian exports, and finance-ministry modelling suggests each additional dollar per barrel of Brent translates into roughly $100 million in tax revenue. Yet the Colombian peso devalued 0.7% against the dollar in the first two trading days of the war, breaking the 3,800-peso barrier, and the Colcap equity index fell 4.42% over the same period — classic emerging-market capital flight. As our reporting on the Colombia fertilizer crisis pushing food inflation higher shows, the Petro government is navigating a balance between oil-revenue gains and agricultural-input shocks.

Chile is unambiguously exposed to the import side. The dollar rose 14.8 Chilean pesos at war onset, reaching 886.8. More alarming for the copper industry — which anchors Chilean exports — is the sulfuric-acid problem. Roughly 20% of Chilean copper processing depends on sulfuric acid imported from China. When Persian Gulf supply chains seized up, China halted sulfuric acid exports to protect domestic users, creating a secondary supply shock for Chilean mining. Chile’s diversified crude import mix reduces outright shortage risk, but peso weakness and input-cost inflation are near-certain through mid-2026.

Mexico’s position is more insulated than most assume. The fourth-largest oil producer in the Americas at roughly 1.6 million bpd, Mexico has negligible dependence on Iranian oil or on Hormuz routing, according to a Banamex assessment cited in regional analysis. Mexico’s IEPS (Special Tax on Production and Services) acts as a consumer-price shock absorber, allowing the government to adjust fuel taxes to offset import-price increases. Still, Mexico imports roughly half of the gasoline it consumes, mostly from the southern United States, and has not escaped the U.S. pump-price surge. President Claudia Sheinbaum has publicly expressed interest in studying Brazil’s biofuel ethanol technology — a tacit acknowledgment that energy diversification has become a strategic imperative.

Venezuela is positioned to benefit modestly — higher oil prices translate directly into higher revenue for Caracas’s constrained oil sector, though production capacity limits how much of the windfall the Maduro government can actually capture. Ecuador and Guyana, the region’s other hydrocarbon exporters, are tracking similar patterns to Colombia: terms-of-trade gains paired with fiscal revenue bumps.

Winners and Losers: A Regional Scorecard

Country Net Exposure Key Data Point Main Channel Brazil Mixed (oil positive, fertilizer negative) Ibovespa +16.35% Q1; urea +35% Oil windfall vs diesel/urea squeeze Argentina Mixed 60% ag exports; Vaca Muerta boost Grain prices vs fertilizer costs Colombia Neutral-positive Colcap −4.42% in first 2 days Crude revenue vs capital flight Chile Negative Peso −14.8 at war onset Copper input (sulfuric acid) Mexico Neutral 1.6 mbpd producer; IEPS buffer U.S. gasoline import exposure Venezuela Positive Higher oil revenue Price effect on constrained output Central America/Caribbean Strongly negative Fuel-import dependent Import bills, FX pressure

The IMF’s April 2026 framing, echoed by Callaway Climate Insights, separates Latin America cleanly: hydrocarbon exporters (Brazil, Colombia, Argentina, Ecuador, Guyana) are relative winners thanks to improved terms of trade and fiscal revenue; fuel-import-dependent economies in Central America and the Caribbean are the clearest losers, facing higher import bills, weaker currencies, rising inflation and fiscal strain. The IMF’s baseline still projects Latin America and the Caribbean to grow 2–3% annually over the next two years, contingent on the conflict remaining short-lived. Our reporting on IMF Spring Meetings and Latin America’s growth outlook with Durigan and Caputo tracks the policy debate.

Trump’s Strategy: Peace Through Strength, or Maximum Pressure?

The Trump administration’s public framing of Operation Epic Fury has moved through three distinct phases. The first, from late February through mid-March, emphasized the destruction of Iran’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities, its navy and its defense industrial base. The second phase, from mid-March through early April, added overt regime-change rhetoric — Trump’s April 7 Truth Social post that “a whole civilization will die tonight” was later defended by Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt as a “negotiating tactic,” but the statement landed as nuclear escalation and moved markets accordingly.

The third phase — post-ceasefire — has been consolidation and leverage. After the April 11–12 Islamabad Talks failed, with Vice President JD Vance leading the U.S. delegation in 21 hours of direct talks that ended without agreement, Trump ordered a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports effective April 13 at 14:00 GMT. The blockade involves more than 10,000 U.S. personnel and applies to all ships entering or leaving Iranian ports and coastlines — distinct from the Strait of Hormuz itself, which remains under Iranian selective control. The New York Times reported on April 14 that the blockade’s practical effect has been uneven, with some ships still transiting the strait while Iranian-port shipping has collapsed.

The core negotiating gap remains the enrichment timeline. At Islamabad, the United States proposed a 20-year suspension of Iranian uranium enrichment; Iran countered with five years. The United States rejected the counteroffer. Iran’s ten-point proposal demands a non-aggression pledge, right to control the strait, acceptance of enrichment, full sanctions lifting, return of $6 billion in frozen assets, U.S. military withdrawal from the region, and compensation for war damages via Hormuz tolls. White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller publicly called the nuclear-weapons red line non-negotiable on April 15, while Trump himself told reporters on April 16 that a peace deal was “very possible” and signaled willingness to return to Islamabad.

Political pressure at home is mounting. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM) has opened a formal probe into whether the Trump administration was adequately prepared for Hormuz closure before launching Epic Fury. U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon heading into the 2026 midterm cycle have become a Democratic talking point. Our reporting on the munitions crisis and cheap drones bankrupting militaries in the Iran War documents a secondary strategic lesson: the cost asymmetry between Iranian drones and U.S. interceptors is reshaping Pentagon planning.

China, Russia and the Multipolar Fallout

The war has accelerated the bifurcation of global oil markets. Russia is the clearest geopolitical beneficiary. According to the IEA, Russian crude exports reached 4.6 million bpd during the peak disruption, with higher prices translating directly into revenue for a government still financing the Ukraine war. China, Turkey, Pakistan and India received selective Iranian-mediated Hormuz passage in exchange for political and commercial concessions, further deepening the non-Western axis that has formed around Iranian oil flows.

For Latin America, the most important consequence is reinforcement of China as the dominant export destination. Brazilian oil exports to China hit a Q1 2026 record as European and American buyers scrambled for alternatives to Middle East crude. Our detailed analysis of Brazil’s record Q1 2026 oil exports to China amid Hormuz disruption traces the cargo flows. The trend extends to soybeans, iron ore and beef. In practice, the Iran War has acted as an accelerant on a trend already in motion: deeper Latin American integration into Chinese-centered supply chains.

Food, Fertilizers and the Global Inflation Echo

The fertilizer dimension of the Iran War may prove more durable than the oil shock itself. Iran produces roughly 15% of global urea. When its export infrastructure is partly destroyed and partly blockaded, and when Qatari LNG — a key feedstock for nitrogen fertilizer — is degraded by 17% for 3–5 years, the world’s agricultural input economics shift. Roughly 60% of Latin American fertilizer exports face demand disruption, and virtually every major food-producing economy in the region is paying more for inputs.

The downstream effects are already showing. Inside Iran, food inflation has reached an estimated 105%. Gulf Cooperation Council states have seen grocery prices spike 40–120% with 70% of food imports disrupted by mid-March. Egypt is absorbing an estimated $10 billion in losses from reduced Suez Canal traffic as ships reroute. The OECD has lifted its 2026 U.S. inflation forecast to 4.2% — a 1.2 percentage point jump from pre-war projections — and the UK outlook is now above 5%. Mexico’s tortilla prices, tied to Brazilian and U.S. corn supply, have become a political flashpoint for the Sheinbaum government.

Brazilian fertilizer economics illustrate the cascade mechanics. Urea is produced from natural gas via the Haber-Bosch process; Qatar is among the world’s largest urea exporters, and the Ras Laffan damage has removed roughly a fifth of Qatari gas-based output for 3–5 years. Moroccan phosphate rock, which Brazil could in principle substitute for Middle Eastern phosphate, faces its own bottlenecks: shipping lanes around the Horn of Africa have become more expensive due to rerouting traffic, and Moroccan producers have their own domestic demand to prioritize. Russia is the one major producer that remains largely accessible to Brazilian buyers, but purchasing Russian fertilizer in volume creates secondary-sanctions risk with the Trump administration. The Lula government has quietly lobbied Washington for exemptions, arguing that agricultural-input access is a humanitarian question rather than a sanctions-evasion one.

Emerging Market Contagion: FX, Bonds and Carry Trades

Latin American currencies have outperformed the broader emerging-markets complex through the war. The Brazilian real strengthened toward 5.15 per dollar despite risk-off episodes, the Colombian peso stabilized after early weakness, and the Mexican peso held its range. HSBC and other major banks have recommended overweight LatAm FX positions relative to Asian and European emerging markets, a reversal of the 2024–2025 consensus.

Crypto markets have reflected the same binary. Bitcoin plunged during the late-March escalation and then rallied sharply on ceasefire hopes. Our analysis of Bitcoin’s $75K move on Iran-deal hopes and the short-squeeze strategy explains how positioning got washed out during the war. The bond market’s story has been similarly bifurcated: U.S. Treasuries saw a flight-to-quality bid through March but gave it back as inflation expectations re-rated higher; Brazilian local-currency bonds performed well thanks to the commodity-export bid on the real.

What Happens Next: The Ceasefire Cliff and the Road to a Deal

The two-week ceasefire announced on April 7–8 expires on April 21, 2026. As of mid-April, a second round of Islamabad Talks is “under discussion but nothing scheduled,” according to the White House. Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi has publicly said the sides were “inches away” from a deal at the first round and blamed U.S. “maximalism” for the breakdown. Trump has oscillated between conciliatory statements and threats. Al Jazeera’s April 8 explainer of ceasefire terms and the Carnegie Endowment’s same-day analysis lay out the key unknowns.

Three scenarios are live. In the benign scenario, a second Islamabad round produces a stopgap framework — partial enrichment limits, phased sanctions relief, Hormuz normalization — and Brent drifts back toward $80 by summer. In the middle scenario, the ceasefire lapses into a frozen conflict: Strait flows stabilize around 5–7 million bpd, with selective Iranian tolling accepted as the de facto regime, and Brent holds in the $90–100 range through 2026. In the escalation scenario, either the ceasefire collapses or Iran rushes to a nuclear breakout; the 400-million-barrel reserve release is largely spent, and Brent could retest $120 or higher with a sharper global recession risk.

For Latin America, the policy prescriptions cluster around a few themes: accelerate fertilizer-input substitution (Moroccan phosphates where feasible, domestic production expansion), deepen energy diversification (biofuels, renewables, Vaca Muerta development), maintain fiscal discipline to protect currency stability, and lean into the China-dominated export pull that the war has reinforced. The IMF Spring Meetings — covered in our report on IMF Spring Meetings on Latin America with Durigan and Caputo — have made these themes explicit.

The Strategic Takeaway for Latin America

The Iran War of 2026 has done three things to Latin America at once. It has delivered a fiscal windfall to the oil exporters, a fertilizer shock to the agricultural exporters (who are often the same countries), and an acceleration of the structural shift toward Chinese-centered trade. The net effect in aggregate, per IMF projections, is a modest growth hit offset by favorable terms of trade — but the distribution of pain and gain within each country is sharp and politically consequential.

For Brazil specifically, the war has validated three decades of investment in biofuels and deepwater oil production. It has also exposed the country’s extreme fertilizer-import dependency as a first-order national security vulnerability. Expect the Lula government — or its successor — to push aggressively for domestic phosphate and urea capacity over the next five years, with potential state-led investment in Mozambican phosphate access as a geopolitical hedge.

For the region more broadly, the Iran War has confirmed that the post-Cold War energy order — cheap oil reliably flowing through the Strait of Hormuz — is gone. What replaces it will be messier, more fragmented, more expensive and more politically charged. Latin America’s resource endowment makes it unusually well-positioned to navigate that world, but only if its governments and its capital markets translate the windfall into durable investment rather than short-term consumption. The next six months — from the April 21 ceasefire expiration through the 2026/2027 crop season — will reveal whether that lesson has been learned.

Investors are already repositioning. LatAm-focused funds have reported inflows at their strongest pace since 2021, with Brazilian mid-cap industrials, Argentine energy names (YPF, Pampa, Vista) and Colombian financials drawing foreign interest. Sovereign spreads across the region have tightened relative to Asian emerging-market peers despite the global risk-off backdrop. The copper complex, anchored by Chile and Peru, has moved higher on both energy-cost dynamics and the expectation that global military rebuilding will require massive copper inputs for electrical systems, munitions and vehicles. Lithium producers in Argentina, Chile and Bolivia — the “lithium triangle” — face a more complex outlook: higher oil prices make electric vehicles more attractive, but global monetary tightening in response to inflation could slow EV rollout.

Finally, the political economy of the war has refocused Latin American foreign policy. Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira has used the crisis to position Brazil as a credible non-aligned broker, echoing Lula’s long-standing “active non-alignment” doctrine. Mexico’s Sheinbaum has called for a negotiated settlement. Argentina’s Milei has been the most supportive of the Trump administration’s approach. Colombia’s Petro and Chile’s Boric have openly criticized the U.S. strikes. The divergence matters: it tells Washington which capitals will cooperate on sanctions enforcement and intelligence sharing, and it tells Beijing which capitals are candidates for deeper Belt and Road integration. The Iran War, in other words, is not just an energy crisis — it is a proxy for the reshaping of the hemisphere’s geopolitical alignments over the decade ahead.

World.title: Costa Rica Wildlife Groups Push Back Against Proposed New Regulation
World.content:
A Costa Rican environmental organization is calling for a halt to the government’s proposed new wildlife regulation, arguing that the draft weakens protections, lacks clear scientific support, and moves forward without new funding for the National System of Conservation Areas, known as SINAC. The group, APREFLOFAS, said the proposal from the Ministry of Environment and Energy, or MINAE, would replace the current wildlife regulation established in Executive Decree 40548-MINAE in 2017.

According to the organization, wildlife management in Costa Rica should be grounded in science and focused on conservation rather than greater flexibility for commercial use. APREFLOFAS said the current regulation was developed between 2015 and 2017 by SINAC with support from specialists, research centers, universities, veterinary experts, and wildlife-focused nongovernmental organizations. It also noted that eight constitutional challenges filed against the 2017 regulation were all rejected by the Constitutional Chamber.

The proposed replacement regulation was opened for public consultation on October 21, 2025, with an initial draft containing 325 articles and 22 annexes. The consultation period ended on November 4, 2025. APREFLOFAS said that 10 business days was too short for a technical measure dealing with wildlife conservation and management. The group said civil society organizations, researchers, professional associations, and specialists submitted roughly 800 observations on the draft.

One of the main points of concern involved provisions that would have allowed possession of five wild parrot species and hybrid macaws. APREFLOFAS said those exceptions remained in the second and third versions of the proposal despite repeated objections over their legality and environmental impact.

After a discussion at the National University, MINAE removed the captivity option for the five bird species in a fourth version of the draft, though it kept the provision for hybrid macaws. The organization also questioned a proposed new management category that would combine rescue centers with noncommercial zoos, saying the public record does not show the scientific criteria behind that measure.

APREFLOFAS also pointed to a November 2025 report from the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Commerce, or MEIC, which issued 44 binding recommendations on the proposal. The report said the draft violated principles of regulatory improvement including legality, transparency, clear rules, legal certainty, and interinstitutional cooperation. The environmental group argued that those concerns, together with unresolved technical questions, show the need for closer review before the regulation advances.

Another major issue raised in the statement is funding. APREFLOFAS said the proposed regulation does not include additional technical, technological, financial, budgetary, or human resources for SINAC. It cited the 2025 State of the Nation report, which found that SINAC’s budget had been cut by 40 percent over the last five years, reducing control, monitoring, and enforcement activities in conservation areas.

The group said any new wildlife regulation should strengthen conservation, be backed by verifiable scientific and technical criteria, and be discussed through a broader and more transparent public process. It also called on MINAE to assign more park rangers, personnel, vehicles, and surveillance resources to protected areas, especially in region

World.title: DENIED
World.content:
Olympic and World Championships long jump silver medallist Wayne Pinnock (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

A decision by World Athletics to deny 11 athletes, including four Jamaicans, the right to switch allegiance to Turkiye has ignited a debate over fairness, athlete rights, and the future of international athletics.

The four Jamaicans affected are Olympic discus champion Roje Stona, Olympic shot put bronze medallist Rajindra Campbell, Olympic and World Championships long jump silver medallist Wayne Pinnock, and triple jump standout Jaydon Hibbert.

In its ruling, the sport’s Nationality Review Panel found that the applications formed part of a “coordinated recruitment strategy” by the Turkish Government, driven by lucrative contracts aimed at boosting the country’s international competitiveness ahead of the 2028 Olympic Games, this according to a release from World Athletics on Thursday.

At its core, the decision represents one of the most forceful attempts so far by World Athletics to clamp down on what it perceives as the commercialisation of national allegiance.

The governing body argued that approving the transfers would undermine “the integrity of international competition” and the principle that athletes should have a genuine connection to the countries they represent.

However, for athlete representatives and legal experts, the move raises troubling questions about consistency and fairness.

Agent Paul Doyle, who represents Stona, described the decision as “nonsensical”, pointing to numerous instances in which similar switches had been approved.

“Athletes have transferred allegiances for decades,” Doyle said. “When you look at the ones approved, even in the past five years, it makes zero sense that these would be denied.”

His concern reflects a broader unease within the sport, whether the rules are being applied evenly, or selectively enforced in response to the scale and coordination of this particular case and the subsequent unease expressed by the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association.

A key issue emerging from the ruling is the panel’s decision to assess the 11 applications collectively rather than individually.

Sports attorney Emir Crowne questioned whether this approach compromised the fairness of the process.

“It raises questions as to whether the athletes were unfairly grouped together as opposed to an individualised assessment of each case,” he said.

Beyond procedural fairness, the decision has sparked a deeper argument, whether the ruling constitutes a restraint of trade.

Veteran agent Cubie Seegobin did not mince words, suggesting the matter could ultimately be settled in court.

“I think it’s a restraint of trade,” Seegobin said, adding that governing bodies must adapt to the realities of a modern, globalised sports economy.

Seegobin also questioned the timing of the decision. World Athletics approved stricter transfer of allegiance regulations on March 19, 2026, with the new restrictions taking effect on March 27, 2026. The applications for the Jamaican athletes were submitted well ahead of those dates.

“They should have let this go through and then implement the new ruling moving forward,” Seegobin argued. “This is going to cause confusion and disruption.”

For the athletes themselves, the consequences are immediate and significant.

Many had already committed to the switch, foregoing opportunities to compete for Jamaica in anticipation of representing Turkiye. The denial leaves them in a state of uncertainty, unable to represent their intended new country and disconnected from their previous national programmes.

Doyle confirmed that Stona, in particular, has been deeply affected.

“He’s not happy, obviously, but he understands that it’s a process, and, hopefully we can get through this and it will work out as favourable as possible for him. You know, honestly, the hope was that he would be eligible right away. That’s obviously not going to be the case now, but he’s pretty devastated,” said Doyle.

While athletes can still compete in non-championship events, including road races and club competitions, the pathway to major championships — the Olympics and the World Championships — is now unclear.

Doyle made it clear that preparations are being made to appeal the decision at “the highest level”, though even this process has drawn criticism.

Crowne pointed out that athletes must first request a reconsideration from the same panel that denied them before potentially escalating the matter to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

“To me, that in itself seems procedurally unfair,” he said. “You have to go back to the same panel and ask them to reconsider before accessing another independent body.”

World.title: Sleepless in Catherine Hall
World.content:
A section of the Catherine Hall community where mud and water settle in the streets because of clogged drains.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — With mud in the drains from recent rains adding to the sludge left by Hurricane Melissa, many residents of Catherine Hall in this western city are afraid to sleep at night.

They are worried they will have to once again head to higher ground as flood waters inundate their homes. The residents say the drains in their community have not been properly cleaned since last October’s Category 5 storm.

“We are in big trouble here, man. The drains are a very important part of this community because if the water is clogged up in there with the nastiness and there is no lead out, it’s going to cause problems,” a nervous Melsha Oates told the Jamaica Observer during a recent visit to the area.

While residents are relieved that there has been progress in removing mounds of debris from their property, each time it rains panic sets in. It is worse if the rains comes when it is dark.

“When rain fall in the nights, you can’t sleep; my mother is 77 and she can’t sleep. We just wake and watch because we missed drowning by this [much],” a resident who gave her name as Stacy said, holding two fingers a hair’s breadth apart.

She wants ongoing work on the West Green leg of the Montego Bay Perimeter Road to go faster, convinced there is a link to the challenges they are facing.

“I’ve lived here from 1995 and this never happen yet and it’s all because, you see that road that they are digging, there is no urgency being placed on it. They’ve blocked the drain to open a different channel and they are not hurrying to do it,” Stacy said.

She lambasted those with responsibility for cleaning the drains as in her view, “everybody has dropped the ball”. There have been promises, she said, but no one comes.

For another resident called Jody, it has been a stressful time since Hurricane Melissa.

“Every time is rains, we go through the same trauma. On Tuesday night it rained and I don’t know if we sleep that night because we are saying what if we are going to flood out again,” she said.

“When it rains, in my lane, it’s either we stay in or we stay out. Our drains are blocked with the mud from the hurricane. Every time it rains that is our reality. Another hurricane season is approaching and we don’t know what to expect because the drains are not clean,” Jody lamented.

She said there have been meetings held and information provided indicates that some help is on the way but, for now, they are still in limbo.

“We don’t know what is happening, we don’t know the plans. Usually we would have tried and do things for ourselves but we have so much repairs to do in our houses,” she said.

She too is worried that another hurricane season is on the horizon and the mud and silt build-up from the last one is still in the drains.

Her mother Dawn spoke of what is it is like living with blocked drains and fear.

“When rain falls, it rough, you can’t come out. The water start block up the place and you can’t come out the house,” she said.

“Because the drains are full, as long as the rain fall the water just come back in the community,” she explained.

When the area is not mired in mud, it is shrouded in dust that competes with mosquitoes to force them to seek shelter inside.

World.title: Chronic law chills pain with I.C.E EP
World.content:
Chronic Law.

After spending 73 days in a US immigration detention centre earlier this year, dancehall artiste Chronic Law is stepping back into the spotlight, not with controversy, but with conviction.

The deejay, born Ackeme Jermaine Campbell, is channelling what was one of the most challenging periods of his life into music, announcing his upcoming EP I.C.E (Inside Cold & Empty) — an eight-track project shaped by survival, faith, and deep introspection.

His apprehension by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (I.C.E) in Florida on January 12, 2026 sent shock waves across the Caribbean and the wider dancehall fraternity. For weeks speculation swirled as fans and industry insiders questioned the circumstances surrounding his detention.

But on March 26 the narrative shifted.

Released without charge, Chronic Law is said to have emerged from the ordeal with a renewed sense of purpose — choosing not to dwell on speculation, but on documenting his experience through his art.

Having teamed up with Grammy-winning producer NotNice on the project, Inside Cold & Empty offers a stark window into the emotional and psychological weight of detention, hinting at themes of isolation, uncertainty, and spiritual endurance.

NotNice, detailing the production process, revealed that much of the groundwork had already been laid before Chronic Law regained his freedom.

“From a production standpoint, the EP was already done. Chronic Law was in jail and he and Bashy spent each day on the phone, Bashy playing the rhythms while Chronic Law was on the other end of the line penning his lyrics. So everything was done: Beats were selected and songs were already written. I came into the project to just refine the beats and add my Midas touch; however, I ended up changing some of the tracks, redoing beats, adding production to each, and doing the final mixing and mastering,” he explained.

The project is a collaborative effort between Notnice Records, Collect Di Bread Entertainment, and 1Law, signalling a strategic alignment aimed at delivering both sonic impact and narrative depth.

Set for release on April 24, 2026, with the lead single, Like Samson, dropping April 17 via ONErpm, the project positions Chronic Law at a defining moment in his career.

For an artiste known for his deeply introspective lyrics and street-rooted storytelling, the project feels like a natural extension of his signature style forged in a level of vulnerability never experienced before.

“Going through that 73-day detention made me even more aware and, at times, more guarded. Everybody had their own opinions and drew their own conclusions, but for me, who truly believes in God, and who truly believes in myself, it became a real test,” Chronic Law said.

“Through it all, I know God was by my side. I had to lean on Him, because without that faith things could’ve gone a completely different direction. Since then, my relationship with God has grown deeper; I find myself having real, personal conversations with Him, venting more, just connecting on a different level,” he continued. “ I.C.E (Inside Cold & Empty) was written to show people that no matter the situation, the obstacles, or the fight you’re facing, you have to stay solid. You can’t lose faith. Believe in Christ, stand firm, and fight for your rights.”

World.title: Ernie Smith, beloved Jamaican singer, has died
World.content:
Ernie Smith

Ernie Smith, whose easy-listening songs ruled Jamaican airwaves during the 1970s, has died. The singer-songwriter, who was ill for some time, passed away at the University of Miami Hospital on Thursday, according to his manager, Joanna Marie Robinson.

Smith’s wife, Claudette Bailey Smith, told Observer Online that he died shortly after suffering “cardiac incidents”. Early this week, she disclosed that he underwent a “surgical procedure” on April 9, two days after being admitted to the hospital and was placed in the Intensive Care Unit.

While the surgery was successful, she said the 80 year-old Smith was “heavily sedated” and placed on a ventilator.

Smith’s laid-back songs, which include Pitta Patta, Duppy Gunman and Life is Just For Living, were a contrast to the militant music of roots-reggae acts like Bob Marley, Peter Tosh and Burning Spear, who dominated the 1970s.

Most of Smith’s hit songs were recorded at Federal Records which was owned by the Khouri family. He was the main artiste at that Kingston company alongside Pluto Shervington, who died in 2024.

Smith had other hits such as I For Jesus and Sunday Coming Down, before migrating to Canada in the late 1970s. After returning to Jamaica in the 1990s, he continued to write and record new songs and became a popular attraction on the live show scene.

In late 2025, he and singer Ed Robinson recorded a version of Pitta Patta which entered the South Florida reggae chart.

Smith was born in Kingston but raised in St Ann. His music career took off in the late 1960s with Ride on Sammy, which was followed by Bend Down.

A major breakthrough came for Smith in 1972 when Life is Just For Living won the Yamaha Music Festival in Japan.

Ernie Smith is survived by his wife, three daughters, two sons and one grandchild.

World.title: Stona ‘devastated’ by allegiance ruling, appeal being prepared – Agent
World.content:
Roje Stona (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Olympian Roje Stona has been left “devastated” after his application to switch allegiance from Jamaica to Turkiye was denied, according to his agent, Paul Doyle, who also confirmed that an appeal is being prepared.

Doyle said the decision came as a surprise, particularly given that similar requests have been approved for other athletes in the past.

“Athletes in the past have been approved, and now all of a sudden, these ones aren’t,” Doyle said during an interview with the Jamaica Observer. “I can speak for Roje because he’s the only one that I represent they’ve really, truly embraced Turkish culture, so to me it doesn’t make sense.”

The ruling means Stona, the Olympic discus champion, will not be immediately eligible to compete for Turkiye as had been hoped, disrupting plans for a seamless transition to his new sporting affiliation.

Doyle indicated that while Stona is trying to remain composed, the outcome has been difficult to absorb.

“He’s not happy, obviously, but he understands that it’s a process,” Doyle explained. “Hopefully, we can get through this and it’ll work out as favourably as possible for him. The hope was that he would be eligible right away. That’s obviously not going to be the case now, but he’s pretty devastated.”

Stona is one of 11 athletes whose applications were rejected by the World Athletics Nationality Review Panel. The list includes fellow Jamaicans Jaydon Hibbert, Rajindra Campbell and Wayne Pinnock.

The other affected athletes are Catherine Relin (Selin Can) Amanang’ole (Kenya), Brian Kibor (Kenya), Brigid Kosgei (Kenya), Ronald Kwemoi (Kenya), Nelvin (Can) Jepkemboi (Kenya), Favour Ofili (Nigeria) and Sophia Yakushina (Russia)

Doyle said the athlete’s camp is not accepting the decision without challenge.

“We’re going to appeal it and see where it can go,” he said. “We’re prepared to take it to the highest level.”

Despite the disappointment, Doyle suggested that Stona remains focused on navigating the process and continuing his preparation as the situation unfolds.

World.title: Cuba ‘ready’ for possible US attack, says president
World.content:
This combination of pictures, created on March 17, 2026, shows Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel (left) and US President Donald Trump. (Photo: AFP)

HAVANA, Cuba (AFP) — Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said Thursday his country was “ready” for a possible United States (US) attack on the communist island following months of mounting pressure from President Donald Trump.

“We don’t want that (confrontation), but it is our duty to be ready to avoid it, and if it were unavoidable, to win it,” Diaz-Canel told thousands of people attending a rally in Havana to mark the 65th anniversary of the failed US invasion of the island at the Bay of Pigs.

Cuba has been bracing for a possible attack following repeated warnings from Trump that Cuba is “next” after he toppled Venezuela’s leader, Nicolas Maduro, and went to war against Iran.

Washington and Havana have held talks on de-escalating tensions, but the discussions between the arch-foes have failed to make significant headway, according to US media reports.

Mariela Castro, daughter of late president Raul Castro, said Cubans “want dialogue” with Washington but “without putting our political system up for debate.”

She said her 94-year-old father — who oversaw a historic 2015 rapprochement with the United States under Barack Obama that Trump later reversed — was indirectly involved in the talks.

Raul’s grandson Raul Rodriguez Castro, a colonel, is reportedly among the negotiators.

Diaz-Canel admitted that the current moment was “very grave” but stressed Cuba’s “socialist” nature, as proclaimed by Fidel Castro on April 16, 1961.

The 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion was launched two years after Castro’s revolutionaries took control of the island and began nationalising US-owned properties and businesses.

Between April 15 and 19, around 1,400 anti-Castro Cuban exiles in Miami, trained and financed by the CIA, landed at the Bay of Pigs, about 250 kilometres (155 miles) south of Havana.

Cuban forces repelled the invaders, inflicting a humiliating defeat on the Americans.

Six decades later, Washington now has Cuba again in its sights.

After Maduro’s capture in Caracas, Trump imposed an oil blockade of Cuba, aggravating the impoverished island’s worst economic and energy crisis in decades.

Diaz-Canel rejected what he referred to as a US portrayal of Cuba as a “failed state.”

Havana largely blames its woes on a US trade embargo imposed shortly after Castro’s arrival to power, still in place today, and the more recent oil blockade.

“Cuba is not a failed state, it’s a besieged state,” he said.

Maria Reguiero, an 82-year-old attending the rally, said that, like in 1961, Cubans were “ready to defend their sovereignty, whatever the price.”

World.title: Cop whose gun ‘went off’ and killed girlfriend slapped with manslaughter charge
World.content:
An undated photo of Jimoy Suckoo who was fatally wounded in a May Pen hotel room on Sunday night by a bullet that came from her cop boyfriend's gun. An investigation is under way.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — A police constable implicated in the fatal shooting of his girlfriend, 20-year-old Jimoy Suckoo, at a hotel in May Pen, Clarendon last year after his gun “went off” has been charged with gross negligence manslaughter.

He has been identified as 28-year-old constable Tavoy Hussey.

The ruling to charge Constable Hussey, handed down by the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP), followed investigations by the Independent Commission of Investigations (Indecom) and the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF).

The cop had been taken in for questioning last year following conflicting reports he shared regarding the January 12, 2025 shooting.

Suckoo, also known as Janay or Nay, was a bartender who lived in Paradise, Westmoreland. At the time of the incident, the deceased had been in a relationship with the constable.

According to a police report, Suckoo and Hussey were at Hotel Versalles in May Pen when she received a single gunshot wound to her chest from the cop’s service weapon, a Glock pistol.

The constable initially said he had placed the pistol on the bed where his girlfriend had been resting. He alleged that his back was turned when he heard a loud explosion, after which he discovered she had been shot in her chest.

According to the report, while at May Pen Police Station the constable gave another account of the incident. In that version he said he had decided to get something to eat and was removing his pistol from his leg holster in order to secure it when the gun slipped from his hand. In attempting to catch the gun, the constable said, he accidentally triggered the firearm which discharged a round in the chamber.

READ: ‘This doesn’t look right’

Hussey was offered bail in the sum of $1.5 million with one to two sureties, and reporting conditions. His next court date is scheduled for September 3, 2026.

Since January 2024, 64 law enforcement officers have been charged in relation to incidents investigated by Indecom. Of that total, eight JCF police officers and one correctional officer were charged in 2026.

World.title: Usain Bolt  and Hublot to release new limited-edition watch
World.content:
Usain Bolt poses with his new watch, The "Big Bang Bang Reloaded Usain Bolt" made in collaboration with Hublot (Photo: Hublot, Usain Bolt Instagram account)

Usain Bolt and Hublot have partnered to release a limited-edition timepiece bearing tributes to the legendary sprinter.

Only 200 versions of the Hublot Big Bang Reloaded Usain Bolt will be produced, bearing the sprinter’s mantra: “Anything is possible, don’t think limits.”

Described as a manifesto in motion and created with the fastest man in history, the watch will be a 44 mm signature edition crafted in black ceramic and carbon, crowned by a polished 18K yellow gold bezel.

The Big Bang Reloaded Usain Bolt is part of a collection unveiled recently, which also features the Big Bang Reloaded Kylian Mbappe, which is engraved with “Trust yourself” and features white ceramic.

In a video on Instagram promoting the timepiece, Bolt said, “This is my watch, can you believe it? Believe it.”

The piece carries yellow and green, along with the black and gold features reminiscent of the Jamaican flag; a second hand shaped like a distinctive lightning bolt and another golden lightning bolt on the back of the watch.

The dial of the Usain Bolt features the numbers 6 5 8 in succession, which, when flipped, reads 9 5 8, a callback to Bolt’s still-standing world record of 9.58 seconds in the 100 metre set on August 16, 2009, at the World Athletics Championships.

The watch will cost around 29,000 Euros or US$30,000.

World.title: Starmer ‘furious’ over Mandelson vetting failures as Labour critics pounce
World.content:
Starmer is facing intense scrutiny over what he and his team knew about Mandelson’s clearance for the top diplomatic post when he was appointed in December 2024.

Olly Robbins was dismissed as head of the Foreign Office Thursday evening after losing the confidence of Starmer and Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper over the row.

Mandelson became U.S. ambassador in February 2025 before being sacked in September over his friendship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Guardian first reported Thursday afternoon Mandelson did not pass his security vetting clearance, but that the Foreign Office overruled the decision.

Starmer ally Darren Jones, the chief secretary to the prime minister, told the BBC on Friday morning that the Foreign and Commonwealth Office had ignored the advice of United Kingdom Security Vetting, the government’s screening agency. “I find this whole situation astonishing,” Jones said in his BBC remarks, adding that he had last night suspended the Foreign Office’s right to ignore security vetting going forward. “That is a failure of state process that was in line with the rules, which I have now changed.”

The continued row about Mandelson is raising fresh questions about Starmer’s leadership. With tough local elections looming May 7, one Labour MP told POLITICO’s London Playbook that “grim inaction is our best option” while a loyalist MP said “this can’t go on for many more months.”

A third MP, also a loyalist and granted anonymity like those above to speak frankly, said “There is absolutely no way he [Robbins] made the decision unilaterally.”

World.title: Defense deals and Thomas Tuchel’s chances: Inside the new Anglo-German bromance
World.content:
The Victorians called Britain and Germany “awkward cousins.” These days, Keir Starmer is trying to revive that Anglo-German amity as part of a broader reset with the European Union. The prime minister has wooed Chancellor Friedrich Merz since the Christian Democrat leader took power in Berlin last year, leading to the signing of the Kensington Treaty nine months ago.

The treaty was designed to fill the gap in bilateral relations after Brexit and give the Anglo-German relationship more power with an increasingly bellicose Russia. But how much influence do Starmer and Merz have over an erratic American President Donald Trump — and can the E3 (the U.K., Germany and France) really influence Trump’s war with Iran?

Host Anne McElvoy talks to Susanne Baumann, Germany’s ambassador to London, in her first interview since she was appointed last September. In a week when the British government received stinging criticism over its defense plans, the ambassador defends Germany’s cooperation on long-range missile and other projects. She also rates England’s chances at this summer’s FIFA World Cup under German coach Thomas Huchel.

World.title: Britain’s bitter assisted dying debate is about to come roaring back to life
World.content:
Da Costa called the plan “extraordinary.” She said: “Last time round, MPs voted to allow the Lords to do their work. This is a very different vote. There will be no ‘off switch’ once it goes to the Lords. MPs will be asked if they’re happy with the bill — with all its deficiencies and all the evidence that has been heard — to become law.”

Opponents of the bill argue that the debates in the Lords have exposed holes in the law that the Commons scrutiny did not. One, Labour peer Luciana Berger, pointed out that the bill has sweeping powers and 59 clauses — far longer than any known private members’ bill, including those that allowed abortion and outlawed capital punishment.

Supporters of assisted dying react outside Parliament on June 20, 2025 as MPs in the House of Commons voted in favour of the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill. | Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images

“This process has shown that we can’t get a bill that is safe,” said Berger. “What are [proponents] saying about the medical colleges in this country — the Royal College of Psychiatrists, the Royal College of Physicians, the Royal College of Medical Examiners, the Royal College of GPs, who all as organizations say they are publicly neutral on the principle of assisted dying, but on this piece of legislation, have very substantive and significant concerns about this bill?” Falconer argued that these concerns had been dealt with during debates in the Lords.

Da Costa added: “Supporters promised to do the work in the Lords last time, they didn’t. Instead, Lord Falconer was looking at Parliament Acts before second reading — requesting government advice. They’ve wanted to do this from the start. It’s smoke and mirrors. They’ve always known that the Lords would never have enough time.” (Falconer described this claim as “completely false” and “rubbish,” saying he only considered the Parliament Acts once the bill was almost certainly doomed, and that while he had accepted some changes to the bill, he hadn’t made promises to change it at the outset.)

Leadbeater insisted she is “extremely open to the idea of making changes … but often people can’t tell you what they want those changes to be.” But Berger countered that “ninety-nine percent of the time, Charlie [Falconer] has rejected every single amendment.”

A prime example of this dispute is an amendment by the former Paralympian Tanni Grey-Thompson, which would require people seeking an assisted death to have a pregnancy test. “This includes 72-year-old men,” said Falconer. “It’s absolutely ridiculous. These are such obvious filibustering techniques.” Berger acknowledged it could have been drafted better, but argued the amendment showed there had been scant consideration of what to do if pregnant women wanted to end their lives. “It’s a really good case in point about how this whole process has been completely inadequate,” she said.

World.title: Cyprus hopes EU summit can do what travel ads can’t: Bring tourists back
World.content:
Now Nicosia is trying to move forward. As holder of the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, Cyprus will host all 27 EU leaders over two days later this month — first in the resort town of Ayia Napa on April 23, then in the capital, Nicosia, on April 24.

For Cyprus, the summit is more than a diplomatic set piece. It is also a giant, high-profile reassurance campaign.

“Above all, it is a vote of confidence to the Republic of Cyprus,” Kostas Koumis, Cyprus’ minister in charge of tourism, told POLITICO. “The organization of a such important event in Cyprus … may definitely spread the message even louder that safety is a top priority.”

The hope is simple: A summit normally associated with security cordons, sleep-deprived aides and bilateral drama might also help sell Cyprus as open, calm and very much still in business.

The leaders themselves are unlikely to swap policy papers for pool loungers. But Antonis Orthodoxou, spokesperson for Cyprus’ tourism industry association ACTTA, said the optics matter.

“Hopefully this [summit] will be the beginning of making the people trust more that Cyprus is safe,” he said. “If you are coming to Cyprus, you’re going to see that the island is nothing to be afraid of.”

World.title: What Orbán’s ouster means for MAGA, Le Pen and Brussels
World.content:
Election night in Hungary was an emotional and teary one … but now, the work begins.

The winners — Peter Magyar’s Tisza party — have the daunting task of reversing years of democratic backsliding that went on under Viktor Orbán’s watch. Meanwhile, Fidesz — and far-right parties across Europe — have some intense soul searching to do to figure out what went wrong in Orbán’s campaign.

Our panel of guests includes POLITICO’s White House Correspondent Eli Stokols and our Senior France Correspondent Clea Caulcutt in Paris, along with Balazs Kos, a Hungarian consultant and expert on EU affairs. Together with host Sarah Wheaton, they dive deeper into what the outcome means for Brussels and the MAGA movement across the pond.

We also speak with Frank Furedi of MCC Brussels, a think tank with links to Orbán’s government. He gives us a breakdown of why he believes the Fidesz campaign failed.
